transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Um, well, I guess what brings me in is that I'm just losing hours of my day to rechecking things. I'm an engineer, so I'm used to being thorough, but... this is different. I keep checking and rechecking file dimensions, my revision notes, and even stuff at home, like my dressing supplies or the door locks. 

It's like I don't feel allowed to just move on to the next task. I have to go through the exact same checking routine enough times until... well, until the anxiety finally drops. It's just taking up way too much of my life right now, and I need to figure out how to stop.

Before you feel the urge to check these things, do you notice specific thoughts or worries popping into your head that feel intrusive or unwanted — like thoughts that something bad might happen if you don't check? Or is it more of a general sense of unease that leads you to check?

It's definitely specific thoughts, not just a general unease. Um, for example, even after I know I’ve cleaned the wound area, or... or reviewed a CAD file at work, this thought just keeps cutting in. It's always this worry that I missed one tiny thing, and that it’s going to turn into a bad infection, or a design mistake that ends up actually hurting someone. And the frustrating part is that no matter how much logic I use, I just... I can’t seem to reason it away.
When you feel that anxiety from the intrusive thought, does the checking actually help bring the anxiety down, or does the anxiety eventually go away on its own even without checking?

Well, I'm not entirely sure if it would ever just go away on its own. I don't think I've ever really... just waited it out without checking. The anxiety gets so intense that I always end up giving in and doing the routine. 

When I do check, yeah, it definitely brings the anxiety down. It gives me this sense of relief, but it's only temporary before the whole thing starts over again. So I guess I don't really know what would happen if I just didn't do it.

When you have these intrusive thoughts about missing something or causing harm, how much distress do they cause you just from having the thought itself — separate from the anxiety about what might actually happen if you don't check?

Um, well, like I mentioned a minute ago about the CAD files or the wound cleaning... the thought itself is really upsetting just because of how stubborn it is. It's incredibly frustrating. I know logically that I did the work right, but that worry just forces its way into my head anyway. The fact that I can't just reason it away or shut the thought off... that alone causes a lot of distress, even before I start panicking about the actual consequences of someone getting hurt. It just makes me feel like I can't trust my own brain.

When you think about your day overall, would you say the checking rituals themselves are the main problem that bothers you and takes up your time, or is it more that these intrusive thoughts keep popping up and forcing you to check in order to manage them?

I think it's really the checking rituals themselves that are the main problem. The thoughts are upsetting, sure, but what actually brings me in here is that I'm losing hours of my day to rechecking things. 

It's the dressing supplies, door locks, the file dimensions at work, my revision notes... I just get stuck. I don't feel like I'm allowed to move on to the next thing until I've gone through the exact same checking routine enough times. I have to keep doing it until that anxiety finally drops. So it's the time I lose to the actual checking that really bothers me the most.

If you could somehow make the intrusive thoughts about missing something or causing harm just disappear completely — but still had to do the checking routines — would that be a major relief for you, or would you still feel just as stuck by having to do all the checking?

Um, I'm not really sure how to answer that. It's... it's kind of hard to picture. I mean, the thoughts are what trigger the checking for me in the first place. 

But if you're saying I still had to spend all those hours doing the actual routines anyway... I think I'd still feel pretty stuck. Because, like I said, it's the time I lose to checking the files and the locks that really messes up my day. So... yeah, I don't really know if it would be a major relief if I was still losing all that time. I guess I just haven't ever thought about it like that.

When you're doing these checking routines — checking the file dimensions, the door locks, the dressing supplies — does it feel like you *have* to keep checking until things feel 'just right' or complete, even if you logically know it's already correct? Or does it feel more like you're fighting against an urge you recognize as irrational?

It's definitely that feeling of having to keep going until it feels right, or until the anxiety finally drops. I know logically that the door is locked or the file dimensions are correct the first time I look. But I still get stuck. Like I was saying before, what really brings me in here is that I'm losing hours of my day to rechecking these things—the dressing supplies, the locks, the files, my notes. I just don't feel allowed to move on to whatever I need to do next until I've gone through that same checking routine enough times. It's not so much fighting an urge, it's just feeling trapped until that specific routine is done and the feeling finally settles.

When you have that intrusive thought about missing something or causing harm — before you even start checking — how much of your day would you say is actually spent just being bothered by the thought itself, versus the time spent actually doing the checking routines?

Honestly, the thought itself doesn't take up nearly as much time as the actual checking. It's more that the thought just... happens, and won't leave. 

Like, even after I know I’ve cleaned the wound area, or I've reviewed a CAD file for work, a thought just keeps cutting in. It tells me that I missed one tiny thing and it’s going to turn into an infection, or a design mistake that ends up hurting someone. And I just can’t reason it away. No matter how much logic I use, the thought stays. 

So the thought itself is pretty quick to pop up, but because I can't talk myself out of it, that's what leads to all those hours I spend actually doing the checking routines.

If we could somehow make the checking rituals stop — so you'd no longer feel the urge to recheck the files, locks, and dressing supplies — but the intrusive thoughts about missing something or causing harm still popped up occasionally, would that feel like a major relief, or would you still feel significantly distressed?

If the checking could just stop? Yeah, I think that would be a huge relief. Honestly, that's the whole reason I'm here. Like I said, what's really ruining my days is losing hours just rechecking things—the dressing supplies, the door locks, the file dimensions at work, my revision notes. 

If I didn't feel like I was forced to go through those same routines over and over until the anxiety finally drops... if I could just have the thought, maybe be a little bothered by it, but then actually move on to the next thing I need to do? That would change everything. The thoughts are annoying, but it's the hours I lose to the checking that makes me feel so trapped.
